summary: The two-pointers technique walks two indices through an array or list, either from opposite ends or in the same direction, to replace nested loops with a single O(n) pass. A sliding window is the same idea applied to a contiguous range.

sections.heading: Opposite ends: pair sum on a sorted array
sections.body: Put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, the left value is too small to pair with anything remaining, so advance left; if too large, retreat right. Each step discards a candidate, so the whole scan is O(n) with O(1) space instead of O(n²).

sections.heading: Same direction: fast and slow
sections.body: A slow pointer marks where the result so far ends and a fast pointer scans ahead. Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place:

sections.heading: Sliding window
sections.body: Keep a window [l, r] and move r forward each step, adjusting l to restore a condition. Fixed size: add the new element, drop the old one. Variable size: shrink while the window is invalid.

sections.heading: Complexity and requirements
bullets: Typically O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
Opposite-end version usually needs sorted input (or a monotonic property).
Each pointer only moves forward (or only inward), so total moves are O(n).

subtopics.title: Linked lists: fast and slow pointers

sections.body: Slow moves one node, fast moves two. If there is a cycle they meet; otherwise fast hits NULL. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. Both run in O(n) with O(1) space.
Start with the widest container. Move the pointer at the shorter line inward, because a narrower container can only be taller if the short side changes. O(n).
Sort, fix the first element, and run opposite-end two pointers on the rest, skipping duplicates. O(n²) overall, versus O(n³) brute force.
Merging two sorted arrays advances one pointer per input; the Dutch national flag uses three pointers (low, mid, high) to partition 0/1/2 in one pass.

bullets: In-place filtering or removal: slow/fast writer and reader.
Contiguous subarray/substring with a constraint: sliding window.
Cycle or middle of a list: fast/slow.

takeaways: Two indices replace nested loops: O(n) time, O(1) space.
Opposite ends for sorted pair problems; same direction for in-place filtering.
Each pointer moves monotonically, which bounds the work.
